subsystems.name: Quantum processor
subsystems.role: the physical qubits that run the sampling circuit.
parts: superconducting transmons, trapped ions or photonic circuits

subsystems.name: Control and readout stack
subsystems.role: shapes the microwave or optical pulses that drive gates and reads out results.

subsystems.name: Cryogenics (solid-state platforms)
subsystems.role: keeps superconducting qubits at millikelvin temperatures.

subsystems.name: Classical simulation stack
subsystems.role: the benchmark the quantum machine must beat.

subsystems.name: Verification and fidelity tools
subsystems.role: produce a number that says how close the machine's output is to the ideal distribution.

subsystems.name: Benchmark suites and reporting
subsystems.role: make claims comparable across machines and vendors.

buildSteps.title: Pick a task that is hard to simulate
buildSteps.detail: Random circuit sampling and boson sampling are chosen because their output distributions are believed costly for classical computers, while being easy to define and check statistically.

buildSteps.title: Design the circuit or interferometer
buildSteps.detail: A circuit of a defined depth on a defined qubit connectivity is fixed in advance, so the classical world can attempt exactly the same task.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the hardware
buildSteps.detail: Gate fidelities, crosstalk and readout errors are measured and tuned; the run is only worth doing when two-qubit gate errors are low enough.

buildSteps.title: Sample many times
buildSteps.detail: The machine is run for millions of shots to build up the output bitstring distribution.

buildSteps.title: Estimate fidelity
buildSteps.detail: Cross-entropy benchmarking compares the observed distribution with the ideal one, giving a single number for how much of the signal is real.

buildSteps.title: Run the best classical algorithms
buildSteps.detail: Tensor-network, sparse-simulation and improved sampling methods are applied to the same circuit, often taking weeks on supercomputers.

buildSteps.title: Compare and publish with caveats
buildSteps.detail: A claim is made only if the classical runtime estimate is far longer than the quantum one, and the assumptions (memory, hardware, algorithm) are stated explicitly.

buildSteps.title: Watch for classical counter-attacks
buildSteps.detail: Follow-up papers frequently shrink or erase the gap, so the claim is treated as provisional until it survives them.

prerequisites.why: advantage claims need tens of qubits with two-qubit error rates low enough that the output is not dominated by noise.
solid-state processors only work at millikelvin temperatures and need thousands of control lines.
the claim is defined relative to the best known classical method, so that method must be genuinely state of the art.
sampling tasks have no known practical use, so beating a classical simulator is not the same as solving a useful problem.
below-threshold error correction has been demonstrated in small experiments, but not at the scale a useful quantum computation needs.

pathway.milestone: random circuit sampling and boson sampling executed on tens to a few hundred physical qubits
pathway.unlocks: a moving frontier that forces classical simulation methods to improve too.

pathway.milestone: benchmarks whose answer can be checked independently, without trusting the quantum device
pathway.unlocks: claims that do not hinge on runtime estimates and assumptions.

pathway.milestone: early fault-tolerant logical qubits running verifiable circuits
pathway.unlocks: a route from sampling stunts to problems with scientific or industrial value.

pathway.milestone: economic advantage on real workloads such as chemistry, materials or optimisation
pathway.unlocks: justification for commercial quantum computing rather than benchmark records.
